summary: Hypothesized effect modifiers for IV alteplase in acute ischemic stroke center on (1) time-to-treatment, (2) patient age, (3) baseline stroke severity (NIHSS), (4) extent of early ischemic change / infarct core on baseline CT, and (5) baseline hyperglycemia / diabetes. These features map to mechanisms that alter the likelihood of reperfusion, the risk of haemorrhagic transformation, and drug kinetics/response, and are supported by trial subgroup analyses and pathophysiologic principles (e.g., 'time is brain', Emberson et al. Lancet 2014; IST-3 subgroup reports).

feature_hypotheses.clinical_interpretation: Elapsed time from stroke symptom onset to IV alteplase administration.
feature_hypotheses.why_important: Earlier thrombolysis consistently increases the probability of meaningful reperfusion and good functional outcome; pooled analyses show a steep decline in treatment benefit with increasing delay ("time is brain").

mechanisms.description: Ischemic penumbra viability declines with time; earlier clot lysis salvages more threatened tissue, increasing chance of recovery (supported by pooled analyses of alteplase trials; Emberson et al., Lancet 2014).
Alteplase acts by enzymatically lysing fibrin in thrombi; older, more organized clots may be less susceptible to fibrinolysis, so later treatment reduces pharmacodynamic effectiveness.

Delay is a proxy for in-hospital system factors (transport, recognition) and possibly for more complex strokes; these correlated factors can amplify the observed interaction between time and treatment effect.

feature_hypotheses.subgroup_implications: Patients treated very early (e.g., <90–180 minutes) likely derive the greatest additional benefit from alteplase; benefit attenuates and may be minimal at long delays (>4.5–6 hours) unless imaging shows salvageable tissue.
validation_suggestions: Test treatment × continuous time interaction in regression (nonlinear terms or splines).
Stratified analyses by time bands (0–90, 91–180, 181–270, 271–360 minutes) as in pooled meta-analyses.
Compare with pooled trial datasets (NINDS, ECASS, ATLANTIS, IST-3) to confirm consistency (meta-regression).
caveats: Onset time may be uncertain (wake-up strokes) causing misclassification.
Imaging selection (penumbral imaging) can modify apparent time interaction — some late patients with salvageable tissue may still benefit.
Residual confounding by prehospital factors may exaggerate association.

feature_hypotheses.clinical_interpretation: Patient chronological age at stroke onset.
feature_hypotheses.why_important: Age relates to brain reserve, comorbidities, and risk of haemorrhagic transformation; several analyses (including IST-3) suggest absolute risks differ with age and that relative benefit may diminish in the very elderly, though some benefit remains.

mechanisms.description: Older brains have less collateral reserve and more leukoaraiosis/microvascular disease—less tissue salvageable after reperfusion, reducing net benefit.
Age-related vascular fragility and blood–brain barrier disruption increase susceptibility to hemorrhagic transformation after reperfusion, increasing harm and reducing net benefit.
Age is a proxy for comorbidities and pre-stroke disability (which modify absolute benefit); trial inclusion patterns and competing risks can create apparent treatment–age interactions.

feature_hypotheses.subgroup_implications: Very elderly patients (e.g., >80–85) may have smaller net functional gains and higher bleeding risk; clinicians should weigh individualized risks, though IST-3 reported benefit even in older subgroups under some analyses.
validation_suggestions: Model treatment × age (continuous) and check for nonlinearity (thresholds).
Perform subgroup analyses in age bands (e.g., <65, 65–80, >80) and compare absolute and relative effects.
Adjust for pre-stroke mRS and comorbidities to separate biological age vs confounding.
caveats: IST-3 deliberately enrolled older patients—generalizability to other datasets may vary.
Age-related associations may reflect unmeasured frailty rather than direct biological interaction.
Relative benefit may persist while absolute benefit declines with age.

feature_hypotheses.clinical_interpretation: Neurological deficit severity measured by NIH Stroke Scale at baseline.
feature_hypotheses.why_important: Severity indexes both the volume/territory of brain affected and the potential for clinically meaningful improvement; treatment may have larger absolute effect in severe strokes but also higher hemorrhage risk.

mechanisms.description: High NIHSS often reflects large-vessel occlusion and larger ischemic territory—there is more tissue to salvage if reperfused, increasing potential benefit.
Very severe strokes have larger core and poorer collateral flow, increasing reperfusion injury and hemorrhagic transformation risk, which can attenuate or reverse net benefit.

NIHSS is correlated with outcome variance; severe group has higher event rates, so absolute benefit may appear larger while relative benefit is variable—this can produce apparent bidirectional interactions.

feature_hypotheses.subgroup_implications: Moderately severe strokes (intermediate NIHSS) may show optimal risk–benefit; very mild strokes have little room for improvement (small absolute benefit), while very severe strokes may have high risk of harm—expect heterogeneity by NIHSS band.
validation_suggestions: Fit treatment × NIHSS interaction (allow nonlinear effects) and examine absolute vs relative risk differences by NIHSS strata.
Analyze recanalization and sICH rates by NIHSS to see mediating pathways.
Compare findings to pooled analyses (e.g., NINDS, IST-3 subanalyses) for consistency.
caveats: NIHSS captures initial deficit but not infarct core or collaterals; two patients with similar NIHSS may differ biologically.
Mild deficits may be overtreated based on imaging or patient values despite small expected benefit.
Reverse causation risk if early deterioration affects measured NIHSS prior to randomization (unlikely but possible).

feature_hypotheses.feature_name: Extent of early ischemic change / infarct core on baseline CT (ASPECTS / visible hypoattenuation)
feature_hypotheses.clinical_interpretation: Radiological estimate of established infarct core or early parenchymal hypodensity on baseline CT.
feature_hypotheses.why_important: Large established infarct core predicts less salvageable tissue and higher risk of hemorrhagic transformation after reperfusion; trials and imaging studies suggest benefit is reduced when core is large.

mechanisms.description: Large infarcted tissue has irreversible injury and degraded vasculature; reperfusion cannot recover dead tissue and may precipitate hemorrhage, reducing net benefit.
Alteplase-induced fibrinolysis may worsen blood–brain barrier disruption in large-core regions, increasing symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage and offsetting functional gains.
Visible early changes correlate with time, stroke mechanism, and severity—some of the apparent interaction may reflect these upstream factors rather than an independent imaging effect.

feature_hypotheses.subgroup_implications: Patients with large early hypoattenuation or low ASPECTS scores are less likely to gain benefit and more likely to be harmed; small-to-moderate cores are likeliest to benefit from alteplase.
validation_suggestions: Analyze treatment × ASPECTS or % hypodense volume interactions; adjust for time and NIHSS.
Use advanced imaging (CT perfusion) where available to separate core vs penumbra effects.
Compare sICH rates by core size to assess mediation of harm.
caveats: CT ASPECTS assessment has inter-rater variability; misclassification can bias interactions.
In IST-3 many scans were non-contrast CT with variable sensitivity for early core—effects may be attenuated.
Some late-presenting patients with small cores (good collaterals) may still benefit despite time delay.

feature_hypotheses.clinical_interpretation: Elevated blood glucose on admission or pre-existing diabetes mellitus.
feature_hypotheses.why_important: Hyperglycemia is associated with worse ischemic injury, increased blood–brain barrier breakdown, and higher risk of hemorrhagic transformation—factors that can reduce the net benefit of reperfusion therapy.

mechanisms.description: Hyperglycemia exacerbates ischemic injury through lactic acidosis and endothelial dysfunction, enlarging irreversibly injured tissue and lowering the likelihood of functional recovery after reperfusion.
Diabetes and hyperglycemia impair microcirculatory reperfusion (no-reflow) and promote blood–brain barrier permeability, increasing symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage risk after alteplase.
Hyperglycemia is a marker of stress response and more severe stroke; as a proxy for stroke severity/physiologic stress it may confound apparent treatment interactions if not fully adjusted.

feature_hypotheses.subgroup_implications: Patients with marked hyperglycemia or longstanding diabetes may experience less functional benefit and higher sICH rates after alteplase; cautious risk–benefit assessment advised.
validation_suggestions: Test interaction of baseline glucose (continuous) and diabetes history with treatment effect, adjusting for NIHSS and time.
Examine sICH rates and functional outcomes in hyperglycemic vs normoglycemic subgroups.
If available, analyze glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) to separate chronic diabetes from acute stress hyperglycemia.
caveats: Hyperglycemia at admission may be stress-induced rather than chronic, with different implications.
Glucose is correlated with other risk factors (age, comorbidity) that must be adjusted for to avoid confounding.
Interventional glucose-lowering trials in acute stroke have not clearly shown improved outcomes, so modification remains uncertain.

cross_feature_patterns: The hypothesized modifiers cluster around two mechanistic domains: (a) tissue viability/reperfusion potential (time, CT core, NIHSS) which amplify or attenuate benefit from successful reperfusion, and (b) host vulnerability to reperfusion injury (age, hyperglycemia) which increase harm risk. Many features are inter-correlated (time ↔ core size ↔ NIHSS), so multivariable interaction models and mediation analyses (e.g., effect of feature on recanalization and sICH) are recommended to disentangle direct effect modification from proxy/confounding.
